281.title: Juzhi's finger
281.hook: a master raised one finger to every question; a boy copied him, and lost the finger (Gateless Gate 3)
281.howItsDone: Zen teachers use Juzhi's finger to warn against imitating a teacher's gestures or words; students are expected to respond to koans in their own way, not by repeating a known answer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Baizhang's fox, five hundred lives for one wrong word, and your line, not blind to cause.

A phrase that sounds wise can go around online in a week. The words spread, but the thing behind them doesn't always come along. At work, the new hire copies the boss's way of talking, the pauses, the catchphrases, and somehow it doesn't land the same. Zen noticed this problem a long time ago. Today's koan is the third in the Gateless Gate, and a warning up front: it's a shocking story. It's about a finger, and the difference between copying and knowing.
screen: `A WISE PHRASE GOES AROUND.` → `COPYING THE BOSS.` → `COPYING VERSUS KNOWING.`

segments.voice: A teacher named Juzhi had one answer. Whenever anyone asked him anything about Zen, he simply raised one finger. That was his whole teaching. He had a young attendant, a boy. One day a visitor asked the boy: what does your master teach? The boy raised one finger, just like Juzhi. When Juzhi heard, he took a knife and cut off the boy's finger. The boy ran out screaming. Juzhi called his name. The boy turned his head. Juzhi raised one finger. And the story says the boy was suddenly awakened. It's hard to hear, and it isn't offered as something to admire or copy. Teachers who discuss it tend to call it a story told to shock, the way a parable exaggerates, and the Buddhist precepts begin with not harming living beings. The Gateless Gate is a teaching collection, not a news report, and nobody knows what, if anything, happened. What the story points at is this. The boy's finger was a copy: the gesture without the seeing behind it. Once the copy was gone, he had nothing to imitate when Juzhi raised his finger. He had to meet it directly, and something opened. At the end of his life, the story goes, Juzhi said he'd received one-finger Zen from his own teacher, Tianlong, and used it his whole life without ever using it up. The finger was never the point. Seeing for yourself was.
screen: `JUZHI RAISED ONE FINGER.` · `THE BOY COPIED HIM.` · `A STORY TOLD TO SHOCK.` · `NOTHING LEFT TO IMITATE.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN FINGER.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you say or do mostly because someone else does it, a phrase, a habit, an opinion you picked up; no judgment, everyone borrows. Ask: if I didn't have their words, how would I say this? Let an answer come, or not, then rest your hands in your lap and feel your own fingers, warm and alive.
Juzhi's finger. A boy copied his teacher's one-finger answer, and only when the copy was gone did he see for himself.
Your line: your own finger. A copied gesture isn't the same as seeing. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 281 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FLAG AND THE WIND.`

282.title: The flag and the wind
282.hook: two monks argue whether the flag or the wind moves; Huineng: your mind moves (Gateless Gate 29)
282.howItsDone: Zen communities honor Huineng as the Sixth Patriarch and study the Platform Sutra, which tells the flag-and-wind story; teachers use the koan to turn students' attention from outside arguments to the mind itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Juzhi's finger, and your line, your own finger: seeing for yourself instead of copying.

A temple courtyard in southern China. A banner flaps on a pole in the wind. Two monks stand under it, arguing, and getting louder. It's like two people at dinner debating whether a movie was any good, and twenty minutes later the argument is clearly about something else entirely. Both are sure they're right. Both are looking out, at the movie, at each other. Neither is looking at what's happening inside. A stranger is standing nearby, a lay worker from the south, and he's about to end the argument with one sentence.
screen: `A BANNER FLAPPING IN THE WIND.` → `TWO MONKS, GETTING LOUDER.` → `THE ARGUMENT THAT ISN'T ABOUT THE THING.`

segments.voice: One monk says: the flag is moving. The other says: no, the wind is moving. Back and forth. The stranger says: it isn't the wind moving, and it isn't the flag moving. Your minds are moving. The two monks were struck silent. The stranger was Huineng, remembered as the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, the Chinese school that became Zen. The Platform Sutra, the book of his teachings, tells this as the moment he was recognized: a poor man from the south, by tradition unable to read, who had quietly received the robe and bowl of the Fifth Patriarch and had been hiding for years. The Gateless Gate keeps it as case twenty-nine. Huineng isn't saying the flag is imaginary, or that wind doesn't exist. Each monk had grabbed one side and was defending it. The movement that mattered was the grabbing: the mind flapping between flag and wind, mine and yours. Huineng turned their eyes around. Then Wumen, in his comment, turns it once more: it isn't the wind, it isn't the flag, and it isn't the mind. In his verse, wind, flag and mind moving are all the same mistake. Even your mind moves can become one more flag to argue about. The koan won't let you stand anywhere. What's left is just looking, before the arguing starts. The Platform Sutra speaks of a mind that doesn't stick to anything. A flapping flag is a good place to look for it.
screen: `FLAG OR WIND?` · `YOUR MINDS ARE MOVING.` · `HUINENG, THE SIXTH PATRIARCH.` · `NOT EVEN THE MIND.` · then, large: `MIND MOVES.`

segments.voice: Watch something that moves, a curtain, a leaf outside, the steam from a cup, or your own belly as you breathe, and notice how quickly the mind adds commentary: it's windy, I like that, I should close the window. Each time, come back to just the movement. Then watch the mind itself moving, thought after thought, the same way, like a flag in the wind.
Huineng. The stranger who stopped two monks arguing about a flag and the wind by saying: your minds are moving.
Your line: mind moves. Not the flag, not the wind, but the grabbing. Day two hundred eighty-two.

283.title: The flower sermon
283.hook: the Buddha holds up a flower in silence; only Mahakassapa smiles, as Zen tells it (Gateless Gate 6)
283.howItsDone: Zen schools tell the flower sermon as the start of their lineage, naming Mahakassapa as the first ancestor after the Buddha, and recite the names of the ancestors from the Buddha onward in their services.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Huineng, the stranger under the flapping flag, and your line, mind moves.

Some of the most important things that pass between two people happen without words. A look across a room when someone says something ridiculous, and you both know. A parent and a teenager in the car, and one small smile that means, we're okay. A best friend who hands you a coffee before you've said a thing. Nobody explained anything, and everything got across. Zen has a founding story built on that kind of moment: a huge crowd, the Buddha, and a sermon with no words at all.
screen: `A LOOK ACROSS A ROOM.` → `ONE SMALL SMILE IN THE CAR.` → `A SERMON WITH NO WORDS.`

segments.voice: The Gateless Gate tells it in case six. The Buddha was on Vulture Peak, the mountain where he often taught, with a great assembly gathered to hear him. He didn't speak. He held up a flower. Everyone was silent, waiting, puzzled. Only Mahakassapa, one of his senior disciples, broke into a smile. Then the Buddha spoke. He said, in effect: I have the treasury of the true teaching, the wondrous mind of nirvana, a gate that doesn't depend on words, a transmission outside the scriptures. I entrust it to Mahakassapa. For Zen this is a beginning: the first link in the chain of teachers, mind to mind, that Zen traces from the Buddha through Mahakassapa to Bodhidharma, who brought it to China, to Huineng from yesterday, and on to teachers today. Now the honest part. This story isn't found in any early Indian text. It first shows up in Chinese Chan writings around the eleventh century, well over a thousand years after the Buddha. Zen tells it as Zen's own story, and many Zen teachers say so openly; the Gateless Gate itself even teases the Buddha for it. Mahakassapa is real in the older texts: in the Pali canon he's a strict forest-dwelling monk who, after the Buddha's death, leads the first gathering to recite the teachings. So the flower sermon is what Zen hears in him. Its point stands whether or not you read it as history: some things are received, not explained. The flower was held up. The smile was the answer.
screen: `A FLOWER ON VULTURE PEAK.` · `ONLY MAHAKASSAPA SMILED.` · `MIND TO MIND.` · `A LATER CHINESE STORY.` · then, large: `THE SMILE.`

segments.voice: If there's a flower or a leaf near you, pick it up; if not, a pen, a spoon or a stone will do. Hold it up in silence, without naming or describing it, and just look, the way the assembly on Vulture Peak looked. If something in you softens, if a smile comes, let it come; if not, keep looking, then lower your hands and breathe.
Mahakassapa. The disciple who alone smiled when the Buddha held up a flower in silence: Zen's story of teaching passed mind to mind.
Your line: the smile. Mind to mind, without a word. That's day two hundred eighty-three.

284.title: Original face
284.hook: what was your face before your parents were born (Gateless Gate 23)
284.howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen 'original face' is often given as an early koan; students hold the question in sitting and daily life and bring their response to private interviews with the teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahakassapa, who smiled at the flower, and your line, the smile.

Count your faces. The one in your passport photo. The one on video calls, slightly brighter than real life. The face for your boss, the face for your oldest friend, the face you make at a baby. The one in the mirror at six in the morning, before you've decided who to be today. Which one is really you? Zen has a question that goes further back than any of them, and it comes from a chase through the mountains. What was your face before your parents were born?
screen: `THE PASSPORT FACE. THE VIDEO-CALL FACE.` → `THE SIX A.M. MIRROR.` → `WHICH ONE IS YOU?`

segments.voice: Remember Huineng from two days ago, the poor man from the south who received the Fifth Patriarch's robe and bowl. The Gateless Gate, in case twenty-three, tells what happened next. Huineng fled south with the robe, and some monks, furious that an outsider had it, chased him. The first to reach him, the story says, was a monk named Ming, once an army officer. He caught up with Huineng in the mountains. Huineng set the robe and bowl on a rock and said: this robe stands for faith; can it be taken by force? Take it. Ming tried to lift it. It wouldn't move, as if it were a mountain. Shaking, Ming said: I came for the teaching, not the robe. Please teach me. Huineng said: don't think good, don't think bad. Right now, at this very moment, what is your original face? Ming woke up on the spot. He had come full of opinions: who deserved the robe, who was right, who was wrong. Huineng asks him to drop all of that and look at what's here before any of the labels. Later Zen teachers put the same question another way, the version in today's title: what was your face before your father and mother were born? It isn't about biology or past lives. It points at what you are before all the faces you've learned to wear, before good and bad, before your name. Teachers don't explain the answer. Like mu, like the flag, it's held and looked into until it looks back.
screen: `A CHASE THROUGH THE MOUNTAINS.` · `THE ROBE WOULDN'T MOVE.` · `DON'T THINK GOOD, DON'T THINK BAD.` · `BEFORE YOUR PARENTS WERE BORN.` · then, large: `BEFORE YOU WERE BORN.`

segments.voice: If there's a mirror near you, look into it quietly; if not, close your eyes and feel your face from the inside, and let the expression you're wearing soften. Let the judgments that come, tired, older, fine, pass without arguing. Then ask gently, without looking for an answer: what was my face before my parents were born?
Original face. What you are before good and bad, before every face you learned to wear: Huineng's question to Ming in the mountains.
Your line: before you were born. Under every face, the one you never had to learn. Day two hundred eighty-four, done.

285.title: Nanquan's cat
285.hook: a hard koan: monks quarrel over a cat; Zhaozhou puts his sandals on his head (Gateless Gate 14)
285.tomorrow: Every day is a good day
285.howItsDone: Zen teachers present Nanquan's cat as a hard koan; some openly discuss the conflict between the story and the precept against taking life, and it is studied rather than held up as an example.

segments.voice: Yesterday: original face, and your line, before you were born. Today's koan is a hard one.

A quarrel, a cat, a sharp blade, and then, strangely, a pair of straw sandals worn as a hat. It's the fourteenth case of the Gateless Gate. Every tradition has stories its own people argue about: stories that don't sit right, that get skipped in the nice version, that make a thoughtful reader put the book down for a minute. Zen has several, and this is one of them. Fair warning: an animal dies in this story. i'll tell it plainly, say what Buddhists themselves say about it, and not pretend it's comfortable.
screen: `A QUARREL AND A CAT.` → `SANDALS WORN AS A HAT.` → `STORIES THAT DON'T SIT RIGHT.`

segments.voice: At Nanquan's monastery, the monks of the eastern hall and the western hall were quarreling over a cat. Who it belonged to, the story doesn't say. Nanquan picked the cat up and held it out. He said: if any of you can say a true word, I'll spare the cat. If not, I'll cut it. No one could answer. Nanquan cut the cat in two. That evening Zhaozhou, Nanquan's student, the one from mu and the washed bowl, came back from a trip. Nanquan told him what had happened. Zhaozhou took off his straw sandals, put them on his head, and walked out. Nanquan said: if you had been there, the cat would have been saved. So what do Buddhists do with this? The first precept is not to take life, and the story seems to break it. Teachers answer in different ways. Some say it probably never happened, a teaching story meant to shock, like Juzhi's finger. Some say Nanquan took the harm on himself to cut through the monks' quarrel. Some modern teachers say plainly that the story troubles them and that no teaching justifies killing. Those who keep the koan say it asks something real. The monks were so caught in owning and arguing that when life itself was on the line, they froze. Zhaozhou's sandals on the head seem to say: you had it upside down. The quarrel was on top and the cat was underfoot. Nobody has one agreed answer. That's why it's called hard.
screen: `EAST HALL AGAINST WEST HALL.` · `SAY A TRUE WORD, OR THE CAT.` · `THE PRECEPT AND THE STORY.` · `THE QUARREL UPSIDE DOWN.` · then, large: `SANDALS ON THE HEAD.`

segments.voice: Let this story, or another story that disturbs you, sit in the room with you, without rushing to fix it, excuse it or throw it out. Notice what it does in the body, a tight jaw, a turned stomach, and breathe with that. You might ask quietly what a true word would have been; if no answer comes, let that be all right, since some stories are carried, not solved.
Nanquan's cat. Monks quarreled over a cat and couldn't say a true word; hearing of it, Zhaozhou put his sandals on his head.
Your line: sandals on the head. A hard story, held honestly. Day two hundred eighty-five.

screen: `DAY 285 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERY DAY IS A GOOD DAY.`

286.title: Every day is a good day
286.hook: Yunmen asks about the days after the fifteenth, and answers himself: every day is a good day (Blue Cliff Record 6)
286.howItsDone: Yunmen's words are a familiar Zen phrase in Japan, where they're brushed as calligraphy and hung in tea rooms; teachers use the case to point to meeting each day fully rather than judging it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nanquan's cat, a hard one, and your line, sandals on the head. Today, something gentler.

Some days are plainly good. The test came back clear. The kids laughed at dinner. Someone you love said the thing you needed to hear. And some days are not. The car won't start. The news is bad. You say the wrong thing and lie awake replaying it. If someone told you on one of those days, every day is a good day, you might want to throw something at them. Yet in Japan those exact words can be found brushed in black ink on scrolls in tea rooms. They come from a Zen teacher who asked his monks a question no one could answer.
screen: `THE TEST CAME BACK CLEAR.` → `THE CAR WON'T START.` → `WORDS ON A SCROLL IN A TEA ROOM.`

segments.voice: The teacher was Yunmen, a Chan master of southern China, remembered for answers so short they land like a splash of cold water. The Blue Cliff Record, in case six, says he told his monks: I'm not asking you about the days before the fifteenth. Tell me something about the days after the fifteenth. Nobody said a word. So Yunmen answered for them: every day is a good day. The fifteenth is the middle of the lunar month, the night of the full moon. Teachers often read it as a picture: before the fifteenth is the time of practice and searching; after it is life after the moon is full, after insight. What's it like then? Every day is a good day. Here's what it doesn't mean. It doesn't mean every day is pleasant, or that you should paste a smile over grief. The good in Yunmen's line isn't the opposite of bad. It's more like: this day, exactly as it comes, is the one you get to live, and there's no better one waiting somewhere else. A day of loss is still a day of your life, and it can be met completely. Some teachers point out that a monk who says every day is a good day still weeps at a funeral. He just doesn't throw the day away. It sits close to the washed bowl from a few days back: Yunmen's line refuses to wait for some realer day. This one is it.
screen: `YUNMEN'S QUESTION.` · `AFTER THE FIFTEENTH.` · `NOT EVERY DAY IS PLEASANT.` · `NO BETTER DAY WAITING.` · then, large: `EVERY DAY IS A GOOD DAY.`

segments.voice: Look back over today so far, the whole thing, not just the highlights: the alarm, the first thing you ate, the small annoyance, the small kindness. Without grading any of it, let it all be today. Then look for one good thing hiding in it, even a tiny one, warm water, a sentence someone said, the fact that you're breathing now, and rest with that.
Yunmen. The Chan master who answered his own question about the days after the fifteenth with a four-word line: every day is a good day.
Your line: this one is it. Hard days are days of your life too. Two hundred eighty-six days now.

287.title: Ordinary mind
287.hook: Zhaozhou asks Nanquan what the way is: ordinary mind is the way (Gateless Gate 19)
287.carry: nothing useless clings to the mind
287.howItsDone: Zen communities treat daily tasks such as cooking, cleaning and gardening as practice, and Wumen's verse on the four seasons from this case is often quoted and brushed as calligraphy.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yunmen, and your line, this one is it. Today closes the week with the plainest koan of all.

People go a long way looking for the spiritual life. Retreats in the mountains. A trip to India. A new book every month, each promising what the last one didn't quite deliver. There's nothing wrong with any of it. But sometimes the looking itself keeps you from finding. Before Zhaozhou was the old master of mu and the washed bowl, he was a young monk with a big question. He took it to his teacher Nanquan, the same Nanquan from the cat. The answer is very short.
screen: `RETREATS, TRIPS, A BOOK EVERY MONTH.` → `THE LOOKING THAT KEEPS YOU FROM FINDING.` → `YOUNG ZHAOZHOU'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Zhaozhou asked: what is the Way? Nanquan said: ordinary mind is the Way. Zhaozhou pressed: then should I aim myself toward it? Nanquan: the moment you aim at it, you turn away from it. Zhaozhou: but if I don't aim at it, how will I know it's the Way? Nanquan: the Way isn't a matter of knowing or not knowing. Knowing is a kind of illusion; not knowing is just a blank. When you really reach the Way beyond doubt, it's wide open, like the sky. Why insist on right and wrong? And the case says Zhaozhou woke up. Ordinary mind isn't a dull mind or a lazy one. It's the mind you already have, before you start trying to become someone more spiritual: getting up, eating, walking, washing the bowl. Wumen's verse goes, roughly: spring has its flowers, autumn its moon, summer its cool breeze, winter its snow. If nothing useless clings to the mind, that's the good season of a life. Look back at the week. Juzhi's finger: your own finger. The flag and the wind: mind moves. The flower sermon: the smile. Original face, before you were born. Nanquan's cat, sandals on the head. Every day is a good day. And now the plainest: ordinary mind. Almost every story this week pointed away from somewhere else and back to right here.
screen: `WHAT IS THE WAY?` · `AIM AT IT AND YOU TURN AWAY.` · `WIDE OPEN, LIKE THE SKY.` · `FLOWERS, MOON, BREEZE, SNOW.` · then, large: `ORDINARY MIND.`

segments.voice: Don't try to meditate well; just sit the way you'd sit waiting for the kettle, noticing the weight of your body, the sound of the room, the breath doing what it always does. There's no special state to reach. If you catch yourself aiming at something, let the aim drop and come back to plain sitting.
Ordinary mind. Nanquan's answer to what the Way is: the mind you already have, before you aim at something special.
Your line: nothing useless clings to the mind. Spring flowers, autumn moon, and this plain day too. That closes the week.

original.note: Chinese píngcháng xīn shì dào: ordinary mind is the Way.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'ordinary mind' means don't bother practicing.
what it means: the Way is found in the mind you already have, not in reaching for a special one.
what a scholar hears: the saying goes back to Nanquan's own teacher Mazu Daoyi, and the case is Gateless Gate 19, with Wumen's four-seasons verse.
